author: antraxia
text:
Hey Pauga! Great to have you here.

After you read for a while you will find that (at least to my current knowledge) they are the same thing. A failed to return FTR limits the resulting price action until it is engulfed thus it usually becomes a flag limit FL. In your chart you have a special type of FL. The one that forms after a significant pole base has been engulfed or the first one that forms after a change in trend (after the last swing has been engulfed and a new FTR is formed). We look for important swings to be engulfed, form a FL and then look for PA on return to that FL or take a Touch Trade (TT) if the conditions are right. Hope this helps some as there was some confusion in the threads as to whether they were the same thing or not. Cheers.

author: thetrendsfriend
text:
Hey,

I do not think that FTR and FTB are the exact same thing. As far as I know, the FTR happens after a break, through a resistance for example. Thereby it is not important if the FTR is after or before the Support, as it is in this case (also see Markepedia article about FTRs). On the chart price breaks (engulfs) the Support, then retraces. The end of the retrace is the FTR. Price then engulfs the first breakout, which is a confiramtion of the breakthrough. When price then returns to the FTR and reacts, it is called FTB.

Would be nice, if an expert could confirm.

author: MaxxAstral
text:
This is one of the best place in this whole Forum, esp article #1 which explains all about FTR. I want to thank Les_Paul for explaining this intrinsic and fundamental element of Price Action.

To sum it up, FTR is simply price Failing to Return to its old Price Action Zone after price Engulf the Limit of the Zone which is denoted by Flag Limits. So naturally the FTR is a decision point that indicates that price is either too expensive or too cheap in that old Price Action Zone hence it must move in the direction of the Engulf ( the hidden signal ), in search for its value. Now in that FTR decision point there are always clusters of unfilled orders left, so when price returns to that FTR and the approach/pressure is not strong then that place is an excellent place to take a position at that FTB.

Thanks

That FTR in the first chart couldn't hold price up much longer as price got capped strongly from the overhead Supply Zone. The cap is strong and wide indicating relatively strong selling pressure compared to the other supplies shown on the chart. Upon breaking south from that cap price did touched the FTR Demand zone for one last push up by taking out that demand, but its attempt is feeble as the cap is too high for the price as confirmed by the second failure to go high. Thus price breaks through the FTR Demand, and goes to the next lower level.
